MOBILEHOME PARK TENANCY (MOBILEHOME RESIDENCY LAW) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Mobilehome Park, LLC

PURPOSE OF THIS MOBILEHOME PARK TENANCY INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's Mobilehome Residency Law (Civil Code sections 798-799.13) as it may relate to the tenancy of a mobilehome space at Sunset Mobile Estates, located at 456 Park Rd, Sacramento, CA 95814, space number Space 12, occupied by Jordan Lee as homeowner, with Acme Mobilehome Park, LLC as management. Under this statutory scheme, the mobilehome itself -- described as 1998 double-wide, 24x60 ft -- is typically owned by the resident, while the space or lot it sits on is rented from the park; this is a materially different tenancy structure from an ordinary residential lease, in which the landlord typically owns both the dwelling unit and the land. The current space rent is 00 per month. This Information Sheet describes the statutory definitions that give this tenancy its structure, the statute's requirements for the park's rental agreement and rules, the statute's own closed list of grounds on which a tenancy may be terminated, the statutory notice periods for a rent increase and for termination, and the statute's protection of a homeowner's right to sell the mobilehome in place. It is a general informational reference, not a rental agreement, a notice of rent increase, a notice of termination, or a determination that any specific ground for termination, notice, or rule applies to this tenancy.

THE STATUTORY STRUCTURE: A RESIDENT-OWNED HOME ON PARK-OWNED, RENTED LAND
The Mobilehome Residency Law defines a mobilehome park tenancy around a split between ownership of the home and ownership of the land. Civil Code section 798.9 defines a "homeowner" as "a person who has a tenancy in a mobilehome park under a rental agreement," and section 798.12 defines that "tenancy" itself as "the right of a homeowner to the use of a site within a mobilehome park on which to locate, maintain, and occupy a mobilehome, site improvements, and accessory structures for human habitation, including the use of the services and facilities of the park." What the homeowner rents, in other words, is the site -- not the mobilehome. Section 798.3(a) separately defines "mobilehome" as "a structure designed for human habitation and for being moved on a street or highway under permit," a structure the statute treats as distinct from the land under it, and section 798.4 defines the "mobilehome park" itself as "an area of land where two or more mobilehome sites are rented, or held out for rent, to accommodate mobilehomes used for human habitation." The park side of the relationship is handled by "management," which section 798.2 defines as "the owner of a mobilehome park or an agent or representative authorized to act on his behalf in connection with matters relating to a tenancy in the park." Together, these definitions describe a tenancy structurally different from an ordinary residential lease: the homeowner typically owns the physical mobilehome and rents only the space beneath it from management, rather than renting a dwelling unit that belongs to the landlord.

REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE PARK RENTAL AGREEMENT
Civil Code section 798.15 requires that the park rental agreement be in writing and requires it to contain a specific list of provisions: "The rental agreement shall be in writing and shall contain, in addition to the provisions otherwise required by law to be included, all of the following." That list begins with "the term of the tenancy and the rent therefor" and "the rules and regulations of the park," and it also requires that "a copy of the text of this chapter shall be provided as an exhibit and shall be incorporated into the rental agreement by reference" -- meaning the Mobilehome Residency Law itself is deemed part of every park rental agreement. The statute separately requires prompt return of a signed agreement: Civil Code section 798.16(b) provides that "management shall return an executed copy of the rental agreement to the homeowner within 15 business days after management has received the rental agreement signed by the homeowner."

RULES MUST BE IN THE RENTAL AGREEMENT, AND STATUTORY RIGHTS CANNOT BE WAIVED
The Mobilehome Residency Law places two specific limits on a park's rules and on the rental agreement that contains them. First, Civil Code section 798.19 makes the statute's protections non-waivable: "No rental agreement for a mobilehome shall contain a provision by which the homeowner waives his or her rights under the provisions of Articles 1 to 8, inclusive, of this chapter. Any such waiver shall be deemed contrary to public policy and void." Second, a park rule is only enforceable as grounds for termination if it is both reasonable and actually part of the rental agreement: Civil Code section 798.56(a)(4) makes it a termination ground only when there is "failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a reasonable rule or regulation of the park that is part of the rental agreement or any amendment thereto."

THE STATUTE'S OWN CLOSED LIST OF GROUNDS FOR TERMINATING A MOBILEHOME SPACE TENANCY
The Mobilehome Residency Law gives management a narrower, more specific set of termination grounds than ordinary residential tenancy law, and states expressly that the list is exclusive. Civil Code section 798.56(a) provides: "A tenancy shall be terminated by the management only for one or more of the following reasons." The seven enumerated grounds are: (1) "Failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a local ordinance or state law or regulation relating to mobilehomes within a reasonable time after the homeowner receives a notice of noncompliance from the appropriate governmental agency"; (2) "Conduct by the homeowner or resident, upon the park premises, that constitutes a substantial annoyance to other homeowners or residents"; (3) conviction of the homeowner or resident of certain enumerated crimes committed on the park premises; (4) "Failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a reasonable rule or regulation of the park that is part of the rental agreement or any amendment thereto"; (5) "Nonpayment of rent, utility charges, or reasonable incidental service charges; provided that the amount due has been unpaid for a period of at least five days from its due date, and provided that the homeowner shall be given a three-day written notice subsequent to that five-day period to pay the amount due or to vacate the tenancy"; (6) "Condemnation of the park"; and (7) "Change of use of the park or any portion thereof, provided" specific advance-notice conditions are met. The Legislature's own stated reason for this narrower list, set out in Civil Code section 798.55(a), is that "because of the high cost of moving mobilehomes, the potential for damage resulting therefrom, the requirements relating to the installation of mobilehomes, and the cost of landscaping or lot preparation, it is necessary that the owners of mobilehomes occupied within mobilehome parks be provided with the unique protection from actual or constructive eviction afforded by the provisions of this chapter."

STATUTORY NOTICE PERIODS FOR A RENT INCREASE AND FOR TERMINATION OF TENANCY
The Mobilehome Residency Law sets its own specific advance-notice periods, distinct from the notice periods that apply to an ordinary residential tenancy. For a rent increase, Civil Code section 798.30 requires that "the management shall give a homeowner written notice of any increase in his or her rent at least 90 days before the date of the increase." For termination of the tenancy generally, Civil Code section 798.55(b)(1) requires written notice, in the manner prescribed for an unlawful detainer notice under Code of Civil Procedure section 1162, giving the homeowner the choice to sell or remove the mobilehome "within a period of not less than 60 days, which period shall be specified in the notice." A termination based on a park's change of use carries longer, tiered notice periods instead of the general 60 days: Civil Code section 798.56(a)(7)(B) requires that, once required permits for the change of use have been approved, "the management shall give the homeowners six months' or more written notice of termination of tenancy" -- or twelve months or more if the change of use requires no local governmental permit.

THE RIGHT TO SELL THE MOBILEHOME IN PLACE, AND THE PARK'S LIMITED APPROVAL DISCRETION
The Mobilehome Residency Law protects a homeowner's ability to sell the mobilehome without removing it from the park, subject to a narrow set of exceptions and a regulated approval process for the buyer. Civil Code section 798.73 provides that "the management shall not require the removal of a mobilehome from the park in the event of the sale of the mobilehome to a third party during the term of the homeowner's rental agreement or in the 60 days following the initial notice required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) of Section 798.55," subject to limited exceptions tied to the home's age, size, condition, and compliance with construction and safety standards; even then, section 798.73(e) requires that "the management shall not require a mobilehome to be removed from the park, pursuant to this section, unless the management has provided to the homeowner notice particularly specifying the condition that permits the removal of the mobilehome." As to the buyer, Civil Code section 798.74(a) allows the park to "require the right of prior approval of a prospective purchaser of a mobilehome that will remain in the park," but section 798.74(c) sharply limits that discretion: "Management shall not withhold approval from a prospective purchase of a mobilehome unless any of the following apply" -- (1) management reasonably determines, based on the purchaser's prior tenancies, that the purchaser will not comply with the park's rules and regulations; (2) "the purchaser does not have the financial ability to pay the rent, estimated utilities, and other charges of the park"; or (3) "the purchaser has committed fraud, deceit, or concealment of material facts during the application process." The statute also builds in a default in the homeowner's favor: under section 798.74(e)(3), "if the management fails or refuses to notify the seller and the prospective purchaser, in writing, of either acceptance or rejection of the application" within the statutory 15-business-day period, "the management shall be deemed to have approved the application of the prospective purchaser."

This Information Sheet describes the statutory definitions that give this tenancy its structure, the statute's requirements for the park's rental agreement and rules, the statute's own closed list of grounds on which a tenancy may be terminated, the statutory notice periods for a rent increase and for termination, and the statute's protection of a homeowner's right to sell the mobilehome in place. The Mobilehome Residency Law defines a mobilehome park tenancy around a split between ownership of the home and ownership of the land. Civil Code section 798.9 defines a "homeowner" as "a person who has a tenancy in a mobilehome park under a rental agreement," and section 798.12 defines that "tenancy" itself as "the right of a homeowner to the use of a site within a mobilehome park on which to locate, maintain, and occupy a mobilehome, site improvements, and accessory structures for human habitation, including the use of the services and facilities of the park." What the homeowner rents, in other words, is the site -- not the mobilehome. Section 798.3(a) separately defines "mobilehome" as "a structure designed for human habitation and for being moved on a street or highway under permit," a structure the statute treats as distinct from the land under it, and section 798.4 defines the "mobilehome park" itself as "an area of land where two or more mobilehome sites are rented, or held out for rent, to accommodate mobilehomes used for human habitation." The park side of the relationship is handled by "management," which section 798.2 defines as "the owner of a mobilehome park or an agent or representative authorized to act on his behalf in connection with matters relating to a tenancy in the park." Together, these definitions describe a tenancy structurally different from an ordinary residential lease: the homeowner typically owns the physical mobilehome and rents only the space beneath it from management, rather than renting a dwelling unit that belongs to the landlord.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code section 798.15 requires that the park rental agreement be in writing and requires it to contain a specific list of provisions: "The rental agreement shall be in writing and shall contain, in addition to the provisions otherwise required by law to be included, all of the following." That list begins with "the term of the tenancy and the rent therefor" and "the rules and regulations of the park," and it also requires that "a copy of the text of this chapter shall be provided as an exhibit and shall be incorporated into the rental agreement by reference" -- meaning the Mobilehome Residency Law itself is deemed part of every park rental agreement. The statute separately requires prompt return of a signed agreement: Civil Code section 798.16(b) provides that "management shall return an executed copy of the rental agreement to the homeowner within 15 business days after management has received the rental agreement signed by the homeowner."

expectedJSON.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law places two specific limits on a park's rules and on the rental agreement that contains them. First, Civil Code section 798.19 makes the statute's protections non-waivable: "No rental agreement for a mobilehome shall contain a provision by which the homeowner waives his or her rights under the provisions of Articles 1 to 8, inclusive, of this chapter. Any such waiver shall be deemed contrary to public policy and void." Second, a park rule is only enforceable as grounds for termination if it is both reasonable and actually part of the rental agreement: Civil Code section 798.56(a)(4) makes it a termination ground only when there is "failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a reasonable rule or regulation of the park that is part of the rental agreement or any amendment thereto."

expectedJSON.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law gives management a narrower, more specific set of termination grounds than ordinary residential tenancy law, and states expressly that the list is exclusive. Civil Code section 798.56(a) provides: "A tenancy shall be terminated by the management only for one or more of the following reasons." The seven enumerated grounds are: (1) "Failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a local ordinance or state law or regulation relating to mobilehomes within a reasonable time after the homeowner receives a notice of noncompliance from the appropriate governmental agency"; (2) "Conduct by the homeowner or resident, upon the park premises, that constitutes a substantial annoyance to other homeowners or residents"; (3) conviction of the homeowner or resident of certain enumerated crimes committed on the park premises; (4) "Failure of the homeowner or resident to comply with a reasonable rule or regulation of the park that is part of the rental agreement or any amendment thereto"; (5) "Nonpayment of rent, utility charges, or reasonable incidental service charges; provided that the amount due has been unpaid for a period of at least five days from its due date, and provided that the homeowner shall be given a three-day written notice subsequent to that five-day period to pay the amount due or to vacate the tenancy"; (6) "Condemnation of the park"; and (7) "Change of use of the park or any portion thereof, provided" specific advance-notice conditions are met. The Legislature's own stated reason for this narrower list, set out in Civil Code section 798.55(a), is that "because of the high cost of moving mobilehomes, the potential for damage resulting therefrom, the requirements relating to the installation of mobilehomes, and the cost of landscaping or lot preparation, it is necessary that the owners of mobilehomes occupied within mobilehome parks be provided with the unique protection from actual or constructive eviction afforded by the provisions of this chapter."

expectedJSON.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law sets its own specific advance-notice periods, distinct from the notice periods that apply to an ordinary residential tenancy. For a rent increase, Civil Code section 798.30 requires that "the management shall give a homeowner written notice of any increase in his or her rent at least 90 days before the date of the increase." For termination of the tenancy generally, Civil Code section 798.55(b)(1) requires written notice, in the manner prescribed for an unlawful detainer notice under Code of Civil Procedure section 1162, giving the homeowner the choice to sell or remove the mobilehome "within a period of not less than 60 days, which period shall be specified in the notice." A termination based on a park's change of use carries longer, tiered notice periods instead of the general 60 days: Civil Code section 798.56(a)(7)(B) requires that, once required permits for the change of use have been approved, "the management shall give the homeowners six months' or more written notice of termination of tenancy" -- or twelve months or more if the change of use requires no local governmental permit.

expectedJSON.body: The Mobilehome Residency Law protects a homeowner's ability to sell the mobilehome without removing it from the park, subject to a narrow set of exceptions and a regulated approval process for the buyer. Civil Code section 798.73 provides that "the management shall not require the removal of a mobilehome from the park in the event of the sale of the mobilehome to a third party during the term of the homeowner's rental agreement or in the 60 days following the initial notice required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) of Section 798.55," subject to limited exceptions tied to the home's age, size, condition, and compliance with construction and safety standards; even then, section 798.73(e) requires that "the management shall not require a mobilehome to be removed from the park, pursuant to this section, unless the management has provided to the homeowner notice particularly specifying the condition that permits the removal of the mobilehome." As to the buyer, Civil Code section 798.74(a) allows the park to "require the right of prior approval of a prospective purchaser of a mobilehome that will remain in the park," but section 798.74(c) sharply limits that discretion: "Management shall not withhold approval from a prospective purchase of a mobilehome unless any of the following apply" -- (1) management reasonably determines, based on the purchaser's prior tenancies, that the purchaser will not comply with the park's rules and regulations; (2) "the purchaser does not have the financial ability to pay the rent, estimated utilities, and other charges of the park"; or (3) "the purchaser has committed fraud, deceit, or concealment of material facts during the application process." The statute also builds in a default in the homeowner's favor: under section 798.74(e)(3), "if the management fails or refuses to notify the seller and the prospective purchaser, in writing, of either acceptance or rejection of the application" within the statutory 15-business-day period, "the management shall be deemed to have approved the application of the prospective purchaser."
